research_question: Can a many-goods response to divine hiddenness count several goods arising from one person’s nonresistant nonbelief without treating their joint realization as an increase in nonbelief-related evil?

argument.title: Many-goods response
argument.paper_title: Divine Hiddenness, Greater Goods, and Accommodation

premises.text: A good may overcome the accommodation strategy if temporary nonresistant nonbelief makes that good sufficiently more valuable.
premises.quote: I suggest that a proposed good might overcome the accommodation strategy if that good is somehow more valuable given temporary nonresistant nonbelief. If nonresistant nonbelief sufficiently increases the value of some good, then it will constitute a sufficient reason for God to allow for nonresistant nonbelief.

premises.text: Multiple goods may arise from a single instance of nonresistant nonbelief without increasing that evil.
premises.quote: This is because nonresistant nonbelief is a single evil (if it can be properly called an evil), and multiple goods may arise from a single instance of evil without that evil increasing.

premises.text: Goods individually less valuable than a relationship with God can collectively make a world containing nonresistant nonbelief more valuable.
premises.quote: Any good at all that is brought about by nonresistant nonbelief will contribute to the overall value of W. This means that the task of identifying goods might actually be relatively simple.

premises.text: Schellenberg’s accommodation strategy does not defeat the many-goods response merely because an individual good can occur within a relationship with God.
premises.quote: But the accommodation strategy is not so devastating against the MGR. Even if some particular good might be possible to acquire within a relationship with God, it might still count in favour of W, rather than W′.

missing_premise.text: If every identified good can be realized within a relationship with God, the many-goods conditions still hold, so that multiple goods without increased evil, collectively outweighing goods, and no defeat by the accommodation strategy together make the many-goods response succeed.

conclusion.text: The many-goods response may succeed even if every identified good can be realized within a relationship with God.

argument.skeleton: B -> A; C; D; ~G |- H -> F

challenged_premise.text: Multiple goods may arise from a single instance of nonresistant nonbelief without increasing that evil.

objection: Belief in God is properly basic. It arises from a faculty that, working as designed, produces it in ordinary circumstances. Nonresistant nonbelief therefore marks that faculty as dulled, and the dulling is itself the evil. Take Maria, raised secular and sincerely open, whose sense of the divine stays silent. Defenders cite three goods from her single case. The first is a freely undertaken search for God, which needs her faculty dulled only until she begins seeking. The second is solidarity with fellow doubters, which needs it dulled through years of shared uncertainty. The third is moral courage without assurance of divine backing, which needs it fully inert at the moment of her ethical crisis, long after her search began. These goods do not share one fixed evil. Each further good requires the malfunction to run longer, reach deeper, or recur at a new point. A truth-aimed faculty failing for longer and more thoroughly is a larger evil. So stacking goods on her nonbelief enlarges the very evil they are meant to offset.

strongest_responses.response: The goods may arise from one shared interval of nonbelief rather than from separate or progressively deeper malfunctions. Search, solidarity, and moral courage can all be consequences of the same period in which Maria doubts.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: This response did not establish that the listed goods share one bounded interval. It conceded that the original premise needs an explicit restriction to such an episode and a measure of its evil.

strongest_responses.response: Several goods can be consequences of a temporally fixed profile of nonbelief, so counting them separately need not itself lengthen, deepen, or repeat the silence. The relevant comparison should be between that profile and its alternatives.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: The objector argued that God determines the profile rather than inherits it, so the comparison must include the shorter period sufficient for the first good. Defender B conceded that life-spread goods cannot be treated as costless merely because they occur within one biographical episode.

open_questions: What individuates a single episode of nonresistant nonbelief: a continuous period, a fixed psychological profile, or a loss of relationship?
Should the evil of nonbelief be measured by malfunction in a properly basic belief-forming faculty, by the duration of a lost relationship with God, or by both?
When goods occur at different times, what makes the longer period of nonbelief necessary for their joint realization rather than merely permitted by it?
What standard of comparability should govern alternatives: must they realize the same goods, or an adequately comparable set of goods with no greater evil?
paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the many-goods response requires a comparative, episode-sensitive account of nonresistant nonbelief: several goods may support a single period of hiddenness only when their joint realization requires no additional nonbelief-related evil relative to available alternatives that secure an adequately comparable set of goods. The case would distinguish genuinely overlapping goods from goods distributed across a life and show why merely redescribing an extended deprivation as one instance does not settle its cost. It would anticipate the strongest reply that all goods can be consequences of one fixed interval, and would need to show either that the interval is necessary for the combined goods or that relevant alternatives impose equal or greater evil.

reasons.coherence: The objection is internally consistent but aims at a stronger claim than c014. The premise is modal, while the objection concerns what particular cited goods actually require. The objection also imports a Reformed-epistemology measure of evil that the original dialectic does not assume.
reasons.robustness: The obvious reply has two parts: the premise is merely possible, and comparative necessity is already a standard theodicy constraint. The direction only half-addresses this by conceding a restricted, comparative version, and it never shows why that version is non-trivial.
reasons.significance: If it succeeded, the paper would at most add an accounting refinement to the many-goods response, namely that distributed goods must be priced by the interval they require. That point is useful but unlikely to change how the hiddenness argument is discussed.
reasons.specificity: The thesis, the overlapping-versus-distributed contrast, and the burden to be discharged against the fixed-interval reply are all stated clearly. However, the key notions of episode individuation and the measure of evil are left as open questions.

assessment.strongest_objection: Premise c014 makes only a possibility claim: multiple goods *may* arise from one instance of nonbelief without increasing it. Showing that some cited goods in Maria's case need longer or deeper nonbelief does not refute that claim. The paper's positive thesis also adds little. Any greater-goods theodicy already requires that each permitted evil be necessary for the goods, with no less costly alternative that secures comparable goods. The many-goods theorist can therefore absorb the point by pricing the whole permitted interval against the whole bundle of goods. The 'increase' then becomes an ordinary cost already on the ledger, not a defect in c014.
assessment.what_it_needs: The paper must show that defenders of the many-goods response actually rely on a non-comparative counting in which life-distributed goods are booked against one fixed evil. It must then show that this counting fails, using an account of episode-individuation and evil-measurement that does not depend on the contested sensus divinitatis premise. Without that, the paper only restates the standard necessity condition.
assessment.summary: A tidy but thin direction: as framed it misreads a modal premise and lands on a version of the standard necessity condition, so it needs a sharper target in the actual many-goods literature before it is a paper.

revision.research_question: Can a many-goods response to divine hiddenness count several goods arising from one person's nonresistant nonbelief without treating their joint realization as an increase in nonbelief-related evil, when the measure of that evil does not presuppose a sensus divinitatis account?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the many-goods response can count several goods from one person's nonresistant nonbelief without increasing nonbelief-related evil only for goods whose required episodes are nested within a single continuous interval, and that goods requiring separated or non-nested episodes must be booked as additional evil. The argument has three parts. First, it shows that defenders of the many-goods response rely on a non-comparative count, in which everything that happens during one long deprivation is booked against one fixed evil, so that the cost of the deprivation is fixed by the life-span and not by what the goods require. Second, it sets out an episode-individuation criterion: an episode is a maximal continuous interval of nonresistant nonbelief, and a good is nested in an episode when its requirements fall wholly inside that interval. The measure of evil is the total extent of the minimal union of intervals that the joint bundle requires, weighted by a neutral depth index, such as the strength of unresisted absence of conviction, that does not presuppose any account of proper basicality. On this measure nested goods add no further episode, so their joint cost equals the cost of the longest-spanning requirement, which is already a cost on the ledger. Distributed goods that need separate episodes, or that need an interval longer than any single requirement, add measured evil. Third, the paper applies this to Maria's case. Her three goods are nested only to the extent that the search, the shared uncertainty, and the ethical crisis lie in one continuous interval. Where the crisis requires a stretch separated from the search by a period of resisting nonbelief, or where the solidarity good requires recurrence, the paper shows that the good's cost is an added episode rather than a re-description of one. The paper concedes that the modal premise survives only in its restricted, episode-sensitive form, and it anticipates the fixed-interval reply by showing that the interval is necessary for the combined goods only when the goods are nested. Where that condition fails, relevant alternatives that secure comparable goods must be shown to impose equal or greater evil.
revision.reply_to_strongest_objection: The paper does not rest on the Reformed-style claim that dulled faculty is itself the evil. It grants the referee's point that c014 is modal and that comparative necessity is a standard constraint, and it shows that the constraint is non-trivial here because the non-comparative count it targets fails. The count books every good from one deprivation against one fixed evil, which hides how much of the deprivation each good actually requires. The paper replaces this with an episode criterion: nested goods share one episode and add no evil beyond the longest requirement, while distributed or recurrent goods add episodes. The measure uses duration and a neutral depth index rather than the sensus divinitatis premise. This shows that c014 holds for nested goods and fails for distributed ones, so the referee's demand for a non-question-begging measure is met.
revision.what_changed: The revision replaces the unrestricted possibility claim with an episode-sensitive, nested-versus-distributed criterion, and it supplies a neutral measure of evil and a non-comparative counting target to make the restricted claim non-trivial.

reasons.coherence: The direction is internally consistent and rightly drops the question-begging sensus divinitatis premise, but it targets a non-modal 'booking' practice rather than c014 as stated, which its own nested case satisfies.
reasons.robustness: The obvious reply is that the paper concedes c014's possibility claim; the direction treats this as a 'restricted form' without explaining why the restriction damages c017 or c021, and it is not shown that the measure is non-ad-hoc.
reasons.significance: At best the paper would supply a useful accounting discipline for many-goods theodicies, but it would not change how the modal argument is assessed.
reasons.specificity: It has a definite criterion (maximal continuous interval, nested requirements, minimal union weighted by a depth index), a worked case, and a three-part plan, though the depth index and the claim about defenders' non-comparative count are underspecified.

assessment.strongest_objection: c014 is an existential modal claim: multiple goods *may* arise from one instance without increasing the evil. The paper's own criterion grants that nested goods sharing one continuous interval add no evil beyond the longest requirement. That establishes the possibility c014 asserts, and c021 is likewise only a 'may'. So the episode-sensitive restriction leaves the argument's modal conclusion intact. The defender simply picks a nested bundle, and the paper refutes nothing the argument claims. It only shows that some bundles (Maria's, under some descriptions) would be costed differently.
assessment.what_it_needs: The paper must show that the goods that do the collective outweighing in c017 (the goods actually cited, not invented nested ones) are typically non-nested, so that restricting to nested goods drains the many-goods response of its aggregate value. It must also defend the interval-additive, depth-weighted measure against a relational view of the evil that is not additive over time.
assessment.summary: A tidy accounting proposal that, by its own lights, vindicates the modal premise it set out to challenge; it needs to show that the goods doing the real outweighing are non-nested before it becomes an objection rather than a footnote.
